\chapter{Tea, Coffee, Milk}
\label{ch:ml-tea-coffee-milk}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can politely ask for tea, coffee or milk in Malayalam, and trace each word back along the road it travelled to get here.}

Ask dayavaayi oru paal, run chaaya's overland Persian route against kaapi's maritime Arabic-Turkish-Italian-English one, and set paal's perfect three-way match against Chapter 15's vellam, which broke from Tamil entirely.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chaaya]{\ml{ചായ} (chāya) — \textquotedblleft{}tea,\textquotedblright{} which walked to Kerala rather than sailed}

\label{lesson:ML-C39-chaaya}



\begin{quote}
Two hearts done. Now the drink you would politely ask for first, in any Kerala home — and a chance to put Chapter 8's \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} back to work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ചായ}} — \emph{chāya} — \textbf{tea}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ദയവായി} \ml{ഒരു} \ml{ചായ}.} — \emph{dayavāyi oru chāya.} — \textquotedblleft{}A tea, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{Dayavāyi} has been yours since Chapter 8; \emph{oru}, \textquotedblleft{}a/one,\textquotedblright{} you have already met attached to \emph{nāḷ} and \emph{maṇi}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ചായ}} traces to Northern Chinese \textbf{chá}, carried overland along Central Asian trade routes into Persian \textbf{\ar{چای}} (\emph{chāy}), and from there into Hindi-Urdu \emph{chāy} and Malayalam \emph{chāya} alike — the same land route most of North and South India took for their word for tea. Tea that instead reached Europe by \textbf{sea} kept a different, southern Chinese form, which is why English says \textbf{tea} and French says \emph{thé} — one leaf, two roads: chai by land, tea by sea.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the two hearts, and the spine node so far}]
\textbf{\ml{ദയവായി} \ml{ഒരു} \ml{ചായ}} leans on the very dative Chapter 6 named, \textbf{‑ikku/‑inu} — the same suffix beside Tamil's \emph{‑ukku}, Telugu's \emph{‑ku}, and Kannada's \emph{‑ge}. This chapter carries both halves of the spine node \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} and \textbf{\ml{ഹൃദയം}}/\textbf{\ml{നെഞ്ച്}} already opened: asking politely, and — if you ask for the wrong thing — repairing with \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dayavāyi oru chāya\textquotedblright{} — a tea, please
  \item the road — \textquotedblleft{}chá … chāy … chāya\textquotedblright{}
  \item land against sea — \textquotedblleft{}chai … tea\textquotedblright{}
  \item please, once more, and its plainer everyday form — \textquotedblleft{}dayavāyi … irikkū\textquotedblright{}
  \item two hearts, once more — \textquotedblleft{}hṛdayaṁ … nenchŭ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for tea, politely. (\emph{Dayavāyi oru chāya}.) Name the three languages \emph{chāya} passed through, in order. (\textbf{Chinese}, then \textbf{Persian}, then \textbf{Hindi-Urdu}, into Malayalam.) Why does English say \textquotedblleft{}tea\textquotedblright{} instead of \textquotedblleft{}chai\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{It arrived by sea}, carrying a different Chinese form.) Which Chapter 6 suffix does \emph{dayavāyi ... enikku} share with Tamil, Telugu and Kannada? (\textbf{The dative} — \emph{‑ikku/‑ukku/‑ku/‑ge}.) What is the repair half of this spine node's word pair? (\textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}}, sorry.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kaapi]{\ml{കാപ്പി} (kāppi) — \textquotedblleft{}coffee,\textquotedblright{} which sailed while tea walked}

\label{lesson:ML-C39-kaapi}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Chāya} travelled overland. This drink took the opposite road — and arrives from further away.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കാപ്പി}} — \emph{kāppi} — \textbf{coffee}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ദയവായി} \ml{ഒരു} \ml{കാപ്പി}.} — \emph{dayavāyi oru kāppi.} — \textquotedblleft{}A coffee, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{കാപ്പി}} comes from \textbf{English} \emph{coffee}, borrowed during the colonial period and reshaped to Malayalam's own consonants and vowels. English's own word for the drink is itself a loan, several times over: Arabic \textbf{\ar{قهوة}} (\emph{qahwah}) became Turkish \textbf{kahve}, then Italian \textbf{caffè}, then English \emph{coffee}, before finally landing in Kerala as \textbf{kāppi}.

Set the two drinks side by side: \textbf{\ml{ചായ}} walked overland from China, through Persia, into North and South Indian speech alike. \textbf{\ml{കാപ്പി}} sailed from Arabia, through Ottoman Turkey and Renaissance Italy, into English, and only then into Malayalam. Two drinks, two opposite roads — one over land, one over sea — meeting on the very same tea-shop counter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dayavāyi oru kāppi\textquotedblright{} — a coffee, please
  \item the long road — \textquotedblleft{}qahwah … kahve … caffè … coffee … kāppi\textquotedblright{}
  \item two drinks, two roads — \textquotedblleft{}chāya,\textquotedblright{} overland; \textquotedblleft{}kāppi,\textquotedblright{} by sea
  \item two hearts, still — \textquotedblleft{}hṛdayaṁ … nenchŭ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for coffee, politely. (\emph{Dayavāyi oru kāppi}.) Which language did Malayalam borrow \emph{kāppi} directly from? (\textbf{English}.) Name the four languages the word passed through before that. (\textbf{Arabic, Turkish, Italian, English.}) Which of this chapter's two drinks travelled by land, and which by sea? (\emph{Chāya} by \textbf{land}; \emph{kāppi} by \textbf{sea}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paal]{\ml{പാൽ} (pāl) — \textquotedblleft{}milk,\textquotedblright{} where Tamil agrees completely}

\label{lesson:ML-C39-paal}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 15's \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}} broke away from Tamil's water-word entirely. This drink, the third in the chapter, does the opposite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} — \emph{pāl} — \textbf{milk}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ദയവായി} \ml{ഒരു} \ml{പാൽ}.} — \emph{dayavāyi oru pāl.} — \textquotedblleft{}A milk, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} is native Dravidian, from \textbf{Proto-South-Dravidian *pāl}, \textquotedblleft{}milk.\textquotedblright{} Tamil keeps the shape \textbf{unchanged}: \textbf{\ta{பால்}} (\emph{pāl}), letter for letter the same as Malayalam. Kannada shows its own regular \textbf{p‑to‑h} sound law here too, giving \textbf{\ka{ಹಾಲು}} (\emph{hālu}) — the identical shift that turns Malayalam's \emph{pōkuka} into Kannada's \emph{hōgu}.

Set beside Chapter 15's finding, this is the mirror image: \textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}} (water) broke from Tamil's \emph{nīr} entirely, choosing a completely different root; \textbf{\ml{പാൽ}} (milk) shows the opposite — perfect three-way agreement in shape, with only Kannada's regular sound law setting its form apart. Two everyday liquids, two entirely different outcomes.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dayavāyi oru pāl\textquotedblright{} — a milk, please
  \item unchanged, then shifted — \textquotedblleft{}pāl … pāl … hālu\textquotedblright{} — Malayalam, Tamil, Kannada
  \item water against milk — \textquotedblleft{}veḷḷam broke away; pāl agrees\textquotedblright{}
  \item three drinks, once more — \textquotedblleft{}chāya, kāppi, pāl\textquotedblright{}
  \item the long road, once more — \textquotedblleft{}qahwah … kahve … caffè … kāppi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask for milk, politely. (\emph{Dayavāyi oru pāl}.) Does Tamil's word for milk match Malayalam's? (\textbf{Yes — exactly}, \emph{pāl} both.) What does Kannada's \emph{hālu} show? (\textbf{The regular p-to-h law.}) Which earlier liquid word broke from Tamil entirely, unlike this one? (\textbf{\ml{വെള്ളം}}, water — Chapter 15.)
\end{tcolorbox}
